title: Block the germ routes: clean hands and a routine that works

say: Block the germ routes: clean hands and a routine that works.
This is the video for module 1 of Home Hygiene and Sanitation: Germs, Clean Hands and a Cleaning Routine.
Most stomach illnesses in our homes, like diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid, are caused by germs that live in human faeces.

panel.heading: Germs travel from faeces to mouth
items: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid: germs from faeces
A healthy-looking person can carry them

say: A germ is a living thing too small to see. So a clean-looking cup or clear water can still carry germs.

panel.heading: Germs travel from faeces to mouth
items: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid: germs from faeces
A healthy-looking person can carry them

say: WHO notes that most people infected with cholera have no symptoms, yet they can pass the bacteria in their faeces.

panel.heading: Germs travel from faeces to mouth
items: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid: germs from faeces
A healthy-looking person can carry them

say: Germs make you ill only when they reach the mouth. Every hygiene habit in this course simply blocks that route.

panel.heading: Germs travel from faeces to mouth
items: Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid: germs from faeces
A healthy-looking person can carry them

say: Health workers use the F-diagram. It shows five routes, all starting with F. The strongest barrier is a clean toilet that keeps faeces in, so germs never escape at all.

panel.heading: Five routes, five barriers
items: Fluids: safe water treatment and storage

say: Fluids. Faeces leak into a well, or a dirty cup is dipped into stored drinking water.

panel.heading: Five routes, five barriers
items: Fluids: safe water treatment and storage

say: Fingers. Hands touch faeces when using the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom, then touch food.

panel.heading: Five routes, five barriers
items: Fluids: safe water treatment and storage

say: Flies land on open faeces, then on uncovered food.

panel.heading: Five routes, five barriers
items: Fluids: safe water treatment and storage

say: Fields: children play where someone squatted. And food carries germs from all the other routes.

panel.heading: Five routes, five barriers
items: Fluids: safe water treatment and storage

say: For example, Bisi lives in a compound in Ibadan where four households share one tap and one toilet. On Thursday morning, three children have watery diarrhoea.

panel.heading: Bisi closes the gaps in her compound
items: List what was shared in the days before
Close every gap, not just one

say: Germs have a waiting period before symptoms. For cholera, it is 12 hours to 5 days. So she looks back days, not just to the last meal.

panel.heading: Bisi closes the gaps in her compound
items: List what was shared in the days before
Close every gap, not just one

say: She walks the routes. One household dips cups into an open water bucket. The toilet door does not close, and flies gather. There is no soap near the toilet.

panel.heading: Bisi closes the gaps in her compound
items: List what was shared in the days before
Close every gap, not just one

say: She does not try to prove the exact cause. She gets a lidded water container with a tap, soap beside the toilet, and a repaired door.

panel.heading: Bisi closes the gaps in her compound
items: List what was shared in the days before
Close every gap, not just one

say: And because watery diarrhoea can be cholera, the children start oral rehydration solution, called ORS, and go to the health centre. Severe cholera can kill within hours.

panel.heading: Bisi closes the gaps in her compound
items: List what was shared in the days before
Close every gap, not just one
panel.rule: Watery diarrhoea in a child: ORS and a health centre.

say: Water alone is not enough. Soap lifts grease and dirt, and rubbing and rinsing carry germs away. Wet your hands and use enough soap to cover every surface.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm
Rinse and dry with a clean towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

say: Rub palm to palm, then each palm over the back of the other hand.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm
Rinse and dry with a clean towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

say: Rub with fingers interlaced, and the backs of your fingers against the opposite palm.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm
Rinse and dry with a clean towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

say: Rub each thumb, then the fingertips in a circle in the other palm. Most people miss these, and they are exactly what touches food and faces.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm
Rinse and dry with a clean towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

say: Rinse, dry with a single-use towel, not your wrapper, and use the towel to turn off the tap.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm
Rinse and dry with a clean towel
Turn off the tap with the towel

say: Most people stop after about 10 seconds. Count slowly to 40, or sing a short song twice.

panel.heading: Handwashing in 40 to 60 seconds
items: Thumbs, then fingertips in the palm

Turn off the tap with the towel
panel.rule: Count slowly to 40 while you rub.

say: For example, Halima in Kano makes a hole near the bottom of a 5-litre jerrycan and hangs soap in an onion net.

panel.heading: Halima's jerrycan station
items: Soap in a net: about 3 bars a month

say: She counts 20 washes from one full jerrycan, so each wash uses 0.25 litres.

panel.heading: Halima's jerrycan station
items: Soap in a net: about 3 bars a month

say: Six people washing at 5 key moments a day. That is 30 washes.

panel.heading: Halima's jerrycan station
items: Soap in a net: about 3 bars a month

say: So she needs 7.5 litres a day, and refills in the morning and again after lunch.

panel.heading: Halima's jerrycan station
items: Soap in a net: about 3 bars a month

say: One bar lasts 10 days, so she buys soap in a pack of three. She places the station between the toilet and the house.

panel.heading: Halima's jerrycan station
items: Soap in a net: about 3 bars a month
panel.rule: Put the station where people already walk.

say: Cleaning removes dirt and many germs with soap and scrubbing.
Dirt protects germs, so cleaning always comes first.
Most of the house only needs good cleaning.
Work top to bottom, and cleanest to dirtiest, with a separate cloth for the toilet.

panel.heading: Clean first. Disinfect only where needed

say: Disinfect where faeces, vomit or raw meat juices may have been.
Follow the label dilution, wear gloves, open the window, and never mix bleach with toilet acids or ammonia, because it can release dangerous gas.

panel.heading: Clean first. Disinfect only where needed

say: To remember.
Block all five routes.
Keep faeces in a safe toilet.
Wash hands the WHO way at the key moments.
Clean before you disinfect.
Wipe door handles, switches and taps every day, and share the weekly work fairly, with bleach tasks kept for adults.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Five routes: fluids, fingers, flies, fields, food
A safe toilet is the first barrier
Handwash 40 to 60 seconds at key moments
Clean first; disinfect only where needed
Wipe high-touch spots daily; share the rota

say: Now map your home on the F-diagram and fix one gap, build and test your handwashing station, and post a cleaning rota where everyone can see it. Continue with the lessons below.

items: Map your home on the F-diagram
